title: The C Standard Library
relevance: SDE interviews and OAs probe whether you can use libc safely—I/O streams, bounded string/memory APIs, robust parsing, and knowing what hosted vs freestanding environments actually provide.

phases.goal: Establish that C is small and relies on libc, and that hosted vs freestanding environments change what the library guarantees.

must_hit.point: The C language itself provides almost no built-in I/O, memory allocation, or string primitives; those come from the C Standard Library (libc).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says C is tiny and names libc/macros/types/functions as the source of printf, malloc, strings, etc.

must_hit.point: A hosted environment (e.g. Linux/Windows/macOS) supplies a full standard library and starts at main; freestanding (embedded firmware, kernels) only guarantees a few essential headers and no default file system or dynamic memory.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts fully furnished OS libc vs bare-metal/kernel with limited headers only.

must_hit.point: Freestanding headers include stdint.h, stddef.h, stdbool.h, limits.h, and float.h; OS-dependent headers like stdio.h and stdlib.h are absent.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists those essential headers and notes stdio/stdlib are not guaranteed freestanding.

must_hit.point: In a hosted program, three text streams open automatically: stdin, stdout, and stderr; disk files are handled via an opaque FILE* holding stream state.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names the three standard streams and describes FILE as opaque with position/error flags.

probes: What is the difference between a hosted and a freestanding C execution environment, and which standard headers are you still guaranteed without an OS?

hints.1: Think about where printf or malloc would send bytes if there is no OS and no screen.
hints.2: Hosted starts at main with full libc; freestanding keeps only a short list of limit/type headers.
hints.3: Name freestanding headers like stdint.h/stddef.h/stdbool.h/limits.h/float.h and say stdio.h/stdlib.h need an OS.

phases.goal: Check concrete libc mechanics: buffering, safe line I/O, snprintf bounds, strtol error reporting, memory copy rules, and related library behaviors.

must_hit.point: Most I/O is buffered; stderr is unbuffered by default so error messages still appear if the program crashes; fflush forces a flush.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions buffer → device on fill/close/fflush, and stderr unbuffered for instant errors.

must_hit.point: Prefer fgets over scanf for line input: fgets can include the newline if there was room; scanf can leave bad tokens in the stream and loop forever on repeated failure.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes read-whole-line-then-parse, and scanf leaving letters after a failed %d.

must_hit.point: snprintf writes at most size - 1 characters, always appends a null terminator, and returns how many characters would have been written if the buffer were large enough (truncation detectable).
must_hit.evidence_hint: States size-1 bound, guaranteed '\0', and return value for would-have-written length.

must_hit.point: strtol reports partial parses via endptr and range errors via errno set to ERANGE returning LONG_MAX or LONG_MIN; atoi cannot distinguish valid "0" from garbage and can invoke undefined behavior on overflow.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Uses endptr/ERANGE/LONG_MAX/LONG_MIN and contrasts silent atoi failure.

must_hit.point: memcpy assumes non-overlapping regions (restrict enables optimization); overlapping copies need memmove, which is defined to be safe.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says overlap → undefined for memcpy; memmove may copy backward when needed.

must_hit.point: strtok mutates the input (delimiters become '\0'), keeps static internal position state, is not thread-safe, and cannot be used recursively.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions mutation, hidden static state, and thread-safety/recursion limits.

must_hit.point: ctype.h classifiers take int so they can accept EOF (usually -1); pass char values as unsigned char or you risk undefined behavior for other negative values.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Links int parameter to EOF/-1 and the unsigned char cast rule.

must_hit.point: assert is for impossible programmer logic bugs, not expected runtime failures; compiling with NDEBUG removes asserts entirely from the binary.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Separates logic bugs vs user/runtime errors and mentions -DNDEBUG stripping asserts.

probes: How does snprintf tell you both that the write stayed in-bounds and whether the result was truncated?
How do you validate with strtol that a string was entirely a number, and how do you detect overflow?

hints.1: Look at the size argument and what the return value means when it is larger than the buffer.
hints.2: Bound write is size-1 plus '\0'; truncation shows up when the returned length needs more space than you gave.
hints.3: For full-number checks use *endptr == '\0' after strtol; for overflow check errno == ERANGE (after setting errno to 0 first).

phases.goal: Force explicit choices among libc APIs that look similar but differ in safety, determinism, or overlap handling.

must_hit.point: Even with a vendor libc, embedded firmware often avoids malloc (non-deterministic time, heap fragmentation on long-running systems) and printf (ROM bloat), favoring static allocation and lightweight formatters.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names non-determinism/fragmentation for malloc and program-memory cost for printf.

must_hit.point: sprintf can overflow the destination; snprintf stops at capacity—like pouring until the bucket’s max mark—so buffer formatting should use snprintf with the real buffer size.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts blind sprintf overflow with sized snprintf truncation.

must_hit.point: strncpy is not a general safer strcpy: if src is longer than n it does not append a null terminator; safer patterns are snprintf(dest, n, "%s", src) or POSIX strlcpy.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States missing '\0' when src exceeds n and names the safer alternatives.

must_hit.point: Choose memcpy for disjoint blocks for speed/optimizations; choose memmove when source and destination may overlap.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Pairs disjoint→memcpy and overlap→memmove without inventing timings.

probes: When would you pick memmove over memcpy, and when is strncpy the wrong ‘safe’ copy API?
Why might you ban malloc and printf in microcontroller firmware even if they link?

hints.1: Ask whether the two memory regions can share addresses, and whether the copy API promises a terminator.
hints.2: Overlap breaks memcpy’s restrict contract; strncpy’s n is for fixed-width packing, not C-string safety.
hints.3: Say memmove for overlap; snprintf/strlcpy instead of strncpy; avoid malloc/printf for timing/ROM reasons on embedded.

phases.goal: Apply libc patterns to safe file reading, robust integer parsing, and bounded formatting under interview pressure.

must_hit.point: Always pair fopen with fclose; missing fclose leaks OS file-table slots and can permanently lose buffered output.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions resource limits and lost buffered writes if never closed/flushed.

must_hit.point: Safe line-oriented file reading: fopen, check NULL and perror, loop fgets into a fixed buffer (e.g. size 256), optionally strip a trailing newline via strlen, then fclose.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks the worked example pattern without inventing extra APIs.

must_hit.point: Robust strtol usage: set errno to 0 first, parse with base 10 and endptr, then branch on ERANGE, endptr == input (no digits), else success and optionally report trailing characters when *endptr != '\0'.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists the three checks in that order from the worked example.

must_hit.point: Never pass raw user input as a printf format string; use printf("%s", user_input) so %s/%n in the input cannot read or write arbitrary stack memory.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the format-string vulnerability and the "%s" wrapper fix.

probes: Walk through reading a text file line by line without gets or scanf, including error and cleanup handling.
Given a string that may have spaces, overflow, or trailing junk, how do you parse it with strtol and classify each failure mode?

hints.1: Start from fopen failure paths and what fgets returns at EOF.
hints.2: Fixed buffer + fgets; strip '\n' with strlen; always fclose; for numbers reset errno and inspect endptr/ERANGE.
hints.3: Mirror the worked examples: perror on open failure, fgets loop, and strtol checks for ERANGE, endptr==input, then trailing *endptr.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Hosted environments give full libc and main; freestanding only guarantees essential headers (stdint/stddef/stdbool/limits/float)—no default filesystem or heap—so PC programs with stdio/stdlib do not port to bare metal unchanged.

tradeoffs.topic: fgets vs scanf for text input
tradeoffs.strong_answer: fgets reads a bounded line (newline kept if it fits) into memory you then parse; scanf is fragile—failed conversions leave bad characters in the stream and can infinite-loop if retried blindly.

sprintf can write past the destination; snprintf takes the buffer size, writes at most size-1 chars plus '\0', and returns the length that would have been written so truncation is detectable—never pass sizeof on a char* to a heap buffer (that yields pointer width, e.g. 8, not the allocation).

atoi silently returns 0 for garbage and has undefined behavior on overflow; strtol exposes endptr for leftover text and sets errno to ERANGE with LONG_MAX/LONG_MIN on range errors—full-number check is *endptr == '\0'.
memcpy is for non-overlapping regions and uses restrict for aggressive optimization; overlapping regions are undefined for memcpy and require memmove.

tradeoffs.topic: malloc/printf vs static/custom I/O on embedded
tradeoffs.strong_answer: malloc brings non-deterministic latency and fragmentation risk on systems that cannot reboot; printf bloats scarce ROM—prefer static allocation and lightweight custom formatting even if a minimal libc exists.

gotchas.trap: Using gets(buffer) from older books for input.
gotchas.correction: gets was removed in C11 because it has no size parameter and will overflow the buffer on a long line—never use it; use fgets with an explicit size.

gotchas.trap: Calling printf(user_input) with untrusted input as the format string.
gotchas.correction: If the input contains %s or %n, printf interprets them and can read/write arbitrary stack memory—always print with printf("%s", user_input).

gotchas.trap: Treating strncpy(dest, src, n) as a safe strcpy.
gotchas.correction: If src is longer than n, strncpy does not append '\0'; it was for fixed-width field packing—use snprintf(dest, n, "%s", src) or strlcpy instead.

gotchas.trap: Passing a plain signed char into isdigit/isalpha/etc.
gotchas.correction: ctype functions take int to allow EOF (usually -1); other negative char values are undefined—cast to unsigned char first.

gotchas.trap: Forgetting fclose after fopen, or assuming buffered fprintf already hit disk.
gotchas.correction: Unclosed files leak OS descriptors and may lose buffered output; flush happens on full buffer, fclose, or explicit fflush—stderr is the one that is unbuffered by default.

gotchas.trap: Seeding assumptions that rand() is fine for security.
gotchas.correction: rand() is deterministic after srand and cryptographically weak—never use it for security or cryptography.

gotchas.trap: Linking math.h code on UNIX without -lm.
gotchas.correction: Floating math often lives in libm, separate from default libc—add -lm (e.g. gcc program.c -lm); also avoid exact == on floats, prefer fabs(a-b) < epsilon.
